title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling, Benchmarks, Runbooks, and Known Issues
author: Alyssa Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference for Redwood Inference: architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release-note highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks used by the runtime team. It is intended for engineers (serving runtime, infra, SRE), performance reviewers, and on-call responders.

Goals and scope

- Provide a single reference describing: the runtime architecture and component boundaries; kernel scheduling algorithms and current production policies; profiling procedures and tooling; benchmarking suite and expected baselines; common runbooks for incidents and maintenance; and an up-to-date list of known issues and workarounds.
- Scope: host + dedicated + private deployments where the runtime binary (runtime-worker) is used. Does NOT include SDK/API client docs (see eng-developer-experience).

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

High-level components

- inference-proxy: HTTP/gRPC ingress, authentication, per-request routing, and request shaping.
- router-service: smart request router that applies routing policy (region, cost tier, model compatibility).
- runtime-worker: the GPU worker process that loads model shards, manages KV cache, performs token generation.
- kernel-scheduler: in-process module inside runtime-worker responsible for selecting optimized kernels and scheduling CUDA streams across attention, matmul, quantized ops.
- batch-coordinator: service that aggregates requests for efficient batching and latency-aware scheduling.
- cache-service: Redis-backed prefix/KV cache with in-memory LRU for hot prefixes.
- telemetry-agent: collects traces, custom metrics, and aggregated perf events to observability.

Service ownership and contact

- runtime-worker, kernel-scheduler, batch-coordinator: eng-serving-runtime (primary). Owners: Alyssa Chen (runtime arch), Diego Rivera (scheduler), Priya Kumar (batching).
- inference-proxy, router-service: eng-platform (secondary integration).
- telemetry-agent: eng-sre (observability integration).

SLOs (production targets)

- 95th percentile tail latency for text generation (1k prompt, 128-generation): <= 350ms for small models, <= 2s for 7B-class models on dedicated GPU pool.
- Token generation throughput: baseline throughput_per_gpu metric >= 15 tokens/ms (A100-40GB baseline) under steady-state batched load.
- Error rate: API 5xx <= 0.05% across hosted clusters.

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies

Design goals

- Maximize throughput while maintaining latency SLOs.
- Adapt kernel selection to model architecture (transformer variant), sequence length distribution, and hardware characteristics (tensor core availability, compute capability).
- Provide graceful degradation: fall back to safe kernels when memory or streaming constraints appear.

Core algorithmic steps (high level)

1. Inspect model metadata and input sequence length distribution (runtime-annotations).
2. Query kernel catalog: prefer fused attention + causal masking kernels for short sequences; use chunked attention kernels for very long sequences.
3. Estimate per-request execution time using profiling-derived cost models (cost_model_v3).
4. Run an online scheduler that balances between: latency-first (low-concurrency streams for low-p99 latency), throughput-first (high-concurrency for batching efficiency), and mixed policies for tiered customers.

Policies and overrides

- Default policy: "latency-adaptive" for hosted API and "throughput-priority" for Dedicated reserved pools.
- Customer tiers can set policy per route via route.config.scheduler_policy: [latency-adaptive, throughput-priority, cost-aware].
- Emergency override: on GPU memory pressure or increased p95 latency, kernel-scheduler auto-switches to safe-kernel-fallback and reduces batch sizes by 20%.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Purpose and tools

- Purpose: collect deterministic microbenchmarks and end-to-end workloads to validate kernel selection, batch sizing, and KV cache effectiveness.
- Tools: perf-trace (internal wrapper), nvprof/nvtx (CUDA traces), runtime-profiler (agent that emits timing buckets), and bench-runner (benchmark harness in 'benchmark-suite' repo).

Procedure (operational steps)

1. Reproduce baseline: run bench-runner --model <model> --sequence 1024 --batch 1 --tokens 512 --gpu-type a100-40 --out=baseline.json.
2. Collect traces: export NVTX_TRACE=1; bench-runner ... | perf-trace collect --out trace.nvtx.
3. Generate kernel selection profile: runtime-profiler analyze --trace trace.nvtx --out kernel-profile.json.
4. Compare against canonical performance: python tools/compare_profiles.py baseline.json kernel-profile.json --threshold 10%.

Key metrics to capture

- Kernel-level latency distributions (per-layer).
- CUDA stream concurrency and stall times.
- Batch packing efficiency (% of full batch tokens scheduled).
- KV cache hit rate and cache eviction churn.

4) Benchmarking suite and baselines

Repository and CI

- repo: git@github.com:redwood/benchmark-suite.git (internal). CI job: benchmark/eval on main executes daily against canary infra.

Canonical tests (examples)

- micro-kernel: micro-bench --model gptx-small --op attention --seq 128 --iters 1000. Expected p50 < 0.45ms on a100-40.
- e2e-latency: bench-runner --model gptx-7b --seq 512 --batch 8 --tokens 256. Target p95 <= 1.1s on dedicated-7b pool.
- burst-throughput: burst-test --duration 60s --rps 200 --model gptx-13b --pool dedicated-large. Expected sustained throughput >= 12k tokens/s.

Publishing results

- Daily CI artifacts are stored in s3://redwood-bench-results/<date>/. Slack notify to #perf-alerts on regressions >10% vs baseline.

5) Release notes (runtime component highlights)

- 2027-08-12 — runtime-worker v3.4.0: Introduced cost_model_v3, improved fused attention kernel for seq<=256 (approx 18% throughput improvement), and added batch-coordinator adaptive windowing.
- 2027-09-20 — kernel-scheduler v2.1.0: Added cost-aware scheduling policy and safe-kernel-fallback to mitigate OOM during quantized attention.
- 2027-11-01 — runtime-worker v3.6.0: Reduced cold-start model load by 28% via lazy shard prefetch and background KV warming.

6) Known issues (current, with workarounds)

- Issue: Occasional CUDA graph capture failure on driver 525.x leading to worker restart (ticket INF-4219). Workaround: set env RUNTIME_DISABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1 in nodes with driver 525 until upgrade to 530+. Planned fix: driver compatibility checks and graceful fallback (Q1 2028).
- Issue: KV cache thrash when multi-tenant short-prefix workloads dominate (high eviction). Workaround: enable per-route pinning for hot prefixes (route.config.kv_pin=true) or increase in-memory cache size to 6GB.
- Issue: Under quantized int8 runs, some matmul kernels produce ~0.5% output delta for gptx-13b on specific prompts. Workaround: route high-sensitivity customers to fp16 model variant via fallback policy.

7) Runtime runbooks (operations)

 a) High p95 latency incident (playbook)

1. Triage: Check dashboard (grafana/runtime-p95-over-time), confirm spike and affected clusters.
2. Check batch-coordinator and kernel-scheduler logs: kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> -c runtime-worker | grep "scheduler" | tail -n 200.
3. If p95 correlates with spike in batch sizes: set batch-coordinator.adaptive_window_ms=5 (lower window) via feature-flag.
4. If OOMs are observed on runtime-worker, enable safe-kernel-fallback by toggling /api/admin/scheduler/override?safe=true.
5. Rollback recent runtime-worker image if deploy coincides with spike: kubectl rollout undo deployment/runtime-worker -n runtime --to-revision=<prev>.
6. Post-incident: run bench-runner locally with captured traces and file incident summary in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/postmortems.

 b) Node maintenance (GPU driver upgrade)

1. Cordon node and drain non-runtime pods: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
2. Set RUNTIME_DISABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1 on node-level if upgrading from driver < 530.
3. Upgrade driver and restart kubelet.
4. Uncordon and monitor runtime p50/p95 for 30m.

8) Team wiki and onboarding checklist

- Quick start for new engineers: clone benchmark-suite, run bench-runner against local dev docker image, read kernel-scheduler design doc (linked).
- Useful dashboards: grafana/runtime-overview, grafana/runtime-kernel-metrics, grafana/runtime-cache-health.
- Pager rotation: eng-serving-runtime on-call is responsible for first response; SRE handles escalation after 15 minutes.

9) Appendix: useful commands and sample configs

Sample route config (YAML)

route:
  id: customer-small-gen
  model: gptx-7b
  scheduler_policy: latency-adaptive
  kv_pin: true
  batch_settings:
    max_batch_size: 16
    adaptive_window_ms: 10

Bench-runner example

- bench-runner --model gptx-7b --seq 512 --batch 8 --tokens 256 --gpu a100-40 --out ./results/7b-e2e.json

Profiling example (quick)

- export NVTX_TRACE=1 && bench-runner --model gptx-small --seq 128 --batch 1 | perf-trace collect --out /tmp/trace.nvtx
- runtime-profiler analyze --trace /tmp/trace.nvtx --out /tmp/kernel-profile.json

Contact and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (team slack: #eng-serving-runtime).
- On-call: see rota in team wiki. For Sev2+ escalate to eng-sre pager after 15 minutes.
